pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–14 years

- **Topic:** The Rock Cycle

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Earth and atmosphere):** pupils are taught "the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks," building on KS2 rock properties and linking to plate tectonics.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-ESS2-1 / MS-ESS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-1, MS-ESS2-4, MS-LS2-3] driven by energy from the Sun and Earth's interior, and construct explanations [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-2].

- **Operational details:** Teach the rock cycle as a CYCLE with no fixed start, driven by two energy sources: the Sun (weathering, erosion, transport, deposition at the surface) and Earth's internal heat (melting, uplift, metamorphism). Fix how each rock class forms: igneous from cooled magma/lava (granite — slow, deep, large crystals; basalt — fast, surface, small crystals); sedimentary from weathered fragments compacted and cemented in layers, often with fossils (limestone, sandstone); metamorphic from existing rock changed by heat and pressure without melting (limestone → marble, mudstone → slate). The key move is TRACING a pathway: any rock can become any other — e.g. granite weathers to sediment → sandstone → buried and heated to metamorphic → melted to magma → igneous again. Anchor geological time: these changes take thousands to millions of years, far beyond a human lifetime, which is why we rarely see them happen.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal). The child describes how each rock type forms with an example, traces a valid multi-step path through the cycle, and explains that transformations occur over geological time driven by surface and internal processes.
bestPractices: Teach it as a genuine cycle with no start or end — emphasise that any rock type can transform into any other given the right conditions, rather than a fixed one-way sequence.
Tie each rock class to its forming process and a concrete example (granite/basalt from cooling magma, limestone/sandstone from compacted sediment, marble/slate from heat and pressure).
Have pupils TRACE multi-step pathways through the cycle, since tracing a valid route is the key assessed skill.
Make geological time explicit and felt (thousands to millions of years) so pupils understand why the cycle is rarely observed directly.
Link the two engines — the Sun (surface weathering/erosion/deposition) and Earth's internal heat (melting, metamorphism, uplift) — to connect with plate tectonics.
keyRepresentations: The rock-cycle wheel/diagram with igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic nodes and process arrows.
Rock-texture cues: interlocking crystals (igneous), layers/fossils (sedimentary), banding (metamorphic).
A crust cross-section showing burial, heat/pressure at depth, and magma rising and cooling.
Example rocks per class (granite, basalt, limestone, sandstone, marble, slate).
A geological-time scale contrasting rock-cycle steps with a human lifetime.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the rock cycle has a fixed start and runs one way, rather than being a cycle any rock can enter and leave.
Believing metamorphic rock forms by melting, when it forms by heat and pressure WITHOUT melting (melting gives igneous).
Assuming rocks form quickly, missing the geological timescales involved.
Confusing weathering (breakdown in place) with erosion (transport of the fragments).
Thinking each rock type is permanent, rather than able to transform into the others over time.

learn.summary: Learners aged 12–14 study the rock cycle as a set of linked processes rather than a fixed one-way sequence, learning that any rock type can transform into any other given the right conditions, over geological time. Core activities centre on transforming a rock and tracing a valid multi-step pathway through the cycle (e.g. granite → sand → sandstone → a metamorphic rock such as quartzite → magma → new igneous rock), tying each rock class to a forming process and concrete example, distinguishing metamorphism (heat + pressure, no melting) from igneous melting, linking surface steps to the Sun's energy and deep steps to Earth's internal heat, and making deep time felt. Supporting work includes classification/matching/sequencing and a reference diagram with texture cues; handling real rock samples is a valuable hands-on complement.

activities.title: Transform and trace a rock through the cycle
feedback: When a learner melts a rock and then cools it, confirm the result is igneous — and point out that melting followed by cooling makes igneous rock, not metamorphic rock.

When a learner applies heat and pressure to limestone and gets marble, highlight that the rock recrystallised WITHOUT melting — that is what makes it metamorphic; the same heat-and-pressure-without-melting step turns sandstone into quartzite and mudstone into slate.
If a learner only ever follows one fixed order, prompt them to find a shortcut, e.g. a metamorphic rock melting straight back to magma, to show the cycle is not a one-way conveyor.

When the learner uses 'weather and erode', note these surface processes are driven by energy from the Sun, while 'heat and squeeze' and 'melt' rely on Earth's internal heat — the two engines that keep the cycle turning.
When the time counter reaches millions of years, connect this to why a nearby cliff looks unchanged across a human lifetime: we see a snapshot, not the process.
activities.rationale: Tracing a valid pathway is the key assessed skill, and the insight that any rock can become any other is best supported by letting learners apply processes and watch the transformation and the loop close. An interactive representation with a live texture redraw and a running geological-time counter makes both the pathway logic and deep time concrete, and sorting steps by energy source links the cycle to the Sun and Earth's internal heat. These interaction examples (process buttons, renaming, texture redraw, time counter, pathway challenge) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism visible, not mandatory features, and this is a proposed activity rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.
Students [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-1, MS-ESS2-4, MS-LS2-3] driven by energy from the Sun and Earth's interior.
learnerActions: Start with a chunk of granite and choose a process to apply to it: 'weather and erode', 'bury and compact', 'heat and squeeze', 'melt', or 'cool'.

Watch the sample transform as each process is applied — granite crumbles to sand, sand becomes layered sandstone, sandstone recrystallises under heat and pressure into a metamorphic rock such as quartzite (note that limestone would instead give marble and mudstone would give slate), melting gives magma, and cooling gives new igneous rock — with the rock renamed and its texture redrawn at each step (interlocking crystals for igneous rock, layers for sandstone, and tightly interlocking recrystallised grains for quartzite, which is usually not banded).
Trace your own chosen path through the loop and record the sequence of rocks and processes you passed through.

Attempt a 'get me from granite to marble' challenge: find and record a valid route (routing through a limestone/carbonate parent to reach marble), and check whether your route is one of several possible paths.
Note the elapsed time counter that ticks up, typically by thousands to millions of years for most steps (lava cooling at the surface can be much quicker), and compare that to a human lifetime.

Sort the processes you used by their energy source: surface steps (weathering, erosion, transport, deposition) driven by the Sun, versus deep steps (melting, metamorphism, uplift) driven by Earth's internal heat.
activities.intendedInsight: The rock cycle has no fixed start or end: material can route between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic forms depending on conditions, and these transformations happen over geological time far beyond a human lifetime, which is why we rarely see them occur. The cycle is kept turning by two energy engines — the Sun powering surface weathering, erosion and deposition, and Earth's internal heat powering melting, metamorphism and uplift.

activities.title: Classify, match and sequence rock-cycle knowledge
feedback: If a learner places marble as sedimentary, note that marble is limestone changed by heat and pressure, so it is metamorphic.
If a learner selects 'melting' as the way to make metamorphic rock, correct it: melting and cooling makes igneous rock; metamorphism is heat and pressure without melting.
Reinforce that granite's large crystals come from slow cooling deep underground, while basalt's small crystals come from fast cooling at the surface.
activities.rationale: Classification, matching and sequencing target the assessable sub-skills of identifying rock types, their formation and ordering a valid path. These recognition tasks build and check vocabulary and categories but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and test their own pathway, so they complement rather than replace the transform-and-trace work.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.
learnerActions: Sort granite, basalt, limestone, sandstone, marble and slate into the three classes: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic.

Match each rock example to its formation process (cooled magma/lava; sediment — rock fragments, shells or minerals settling out of water — compacted and cemented; existing rock changed by heat and pressure without melting).
Order the steps of a granite-to-new-igneous-rock journey into a valid sequence.
Answer: which process makes metamorphic rock? (heat + pressure, without melting).
For granite and basalt, decide which cooled slowly at depth (large crystals) and which cooled fast at the surface (small crystals).
activities.intendedInsight: Each rock class is tied to a specific forming process and concrete example, and a valid cycle path is an ordered sequence of those processes.

activities.title: Explore a rock-cycle diagram and rock textures
feedback: When a learner identifies banding, prompt them to link it to heat and pressure acting on an existing rock.
If a learner sees layers or a fossil, connect this to sediment being deposited and compacted over time.
When handling samples, encourage learners to state which class and forming process each specimen shows and why.
activities.rationale: A reference diagram with texture photos and a crust cross-section is a strong vocabulary and spatial anchor, and real samples give a tactile experience of the texture cues. These are supports for the core transform-and-trace skill: a fixed diagram shows the map but does not by itself let a learner build and test their own route, so it is used alongside the interactive and hands-on work.
learnerActions: Tap each rock type and each arrow on a rock-cycle wheel to reveal the process it represents, an example rock, and a photo of its texture.

Compare texture cues across classes: interlocking crystals, large or too small to see (igneous); layers, rounded grains or fossils (sedimentary); banding or foliation in some metamorphic rocks (e.g. gneiss), thin splitting sheets in slate, and a sugary mass of interlocking crystals in marble or quartzite. Note that marble and quartzite also have interlocking crystals, so use more than one cue.
Use a crust cross-section view to see where burial, heat and pressure at depth, and rising/cooling magma occur, and how crystal size relates to cooling depth.
Where possible, handle real rock samples (granite, basalt, limestone, sandstone, marble, slate) and match each to its class using the texture cues.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks carry visible evidence of how they formed, and a diagram plus real samples anchors the vocabulary, processes and spatial setting (depth of burial, cooling) of the cycle.

constraints: Teach the rock cycle as a genuine cycle with no fixed start or end: any rock type can transform into any other given the right conditions.

Metamorphic rock forms from existing rock changed by heat AND pressure WITHOUT melting (e.g. limestone → marble, mudstone → slate, sandstone → quartzite); melting followed by cooling produces igneous rock. Keep these two contrasted and keep the metamorphic pairings accurate.
Link the cycle's two energy engines: the Sun drives surface weathering, erosion, transport and deposition, while Earth's internal heat drives melting, metamorphism and uplift.

Make geological time explicit: most rock-cycle changes take thousands to millions of years (although some steps, such as lava cooling at the surface, can happen in days to years), which is why we mostly observe snapshots rather than the process.
Distinguish weathering (breakdown of rock in place) from erosion (transport of the fragments).

Classification, matching, sequencing and multiple-choice tasks check recognition and vocabulary but do not elicit independent construction of a pathway; include a transform-and-trace or written route-tracing task for that.

A fixed diagram and photos are a useful reference and can teach texture cues and vocabulary, but they do not let a learner trace and test their own pathway; treat them as a complement, not a substitute.
Real rock samples give tactile experience of textures; interactive and physical media offer different experiences and both are valuable — neither is presented as universally necessary.
Full attainment requires describing a specific route BETWEEN rock types AND invoking the vast timescale; naming the three types alone is not sufficient.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists NGSS MS-ESS2-1 as not verified (verified:false) and the DfE KS3 claim as verified:true; original row confidence is marked 'high'. No new verification has been performed here.

The original design notes paired the metamorphic step for sandstone with 'slate/marble', which is geologically inaccurate (slate forms from mudstone, marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone). This was corrected to quartzite in learner-facing text; the original simplification is recorded here and in the audit's uncertain list, not presented as a valid learner option.

The 'granite to marble' challenge follows the source pedagogy's 'any rock can become any other' framing. Reaching marble specifically requires routing through a limestone/carbonate parent over geological time, because granite-derived silica sediment yields sandstone/quartzite; the learner action now makes this routing explicit so the challenge stays geologically coherent.

The two energy engines (Sun driving surface processes; Earth's internal heat driving melting/metamorphism/uplift) were present in the source pedagogy and cited via the NGSS claim but were not taught in the earlier candidate; they have been added to activity[0], a constraint and the audit.

The original marked a 3D crust cross-section as 'possible' and open conversation as 'poor fit' for the transform-and-trace skill; these were catalog fit rankings, not established efficacy claims. The spatial cross-section content has been retained as a supporting exploration, and a geological-time 'geologist chat' is noted as optional light enrichment of the deep-time strand rather than discarded.

Claims in the source that 'static reveals cannot let the child trace their own pathway' and that 2D delivers the learning 'as well or better than 3D at lower cost' are catalog preferences, not verified comparative efficacy; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

Self-audit: formation facts (granite = slow/deep/large crystals; basalt = fast/surface/small crystals; metamorphism = heat + pressure without melting; melting + cooling = igneous) are internally consistent across pedagogy and assessment fields and were preserved. No arithmetic or force/motion content present.

probeDeeper: Trace a single grain of sand from a mountain to a sedimentary rock and then to a metamorphic one — what happens at each step?
Marble comes from limestone by heat and pressure. Was it melted? How is that different from how granite forms?
If rocks really change, why has the cliff near my house looked the same my whole life?
Could a metamorphic rock become igneous without first becoming sedimentary? How?
assess.correctAnswer: Not true — over GEOLOGICAL time (millions of years) rock is continually recycled. Granite could be weathered into grains, the grains compacted into sedimentary rock, then heated and squeezed into metamorphic rock, or melted to magma and cooled into new igneous rock. We never watch it because the processes are unimaginably slow compared with a human life. Full marks describe a route BETWEEN types AND invoke the vast timescale.

errorPatterns.pattern: rocks are permanent and unchanging ('a rock is always the same rock')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce deep time and the cycle: weathering, sedimentation, heat/pressure and melting continually remake rock. Trace one grain through several forms.
errorPatterns.distractor: True — granite stays granite forever; rocks never change into other kinds.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies any rock can become another type; treats rock as fixed

errorPatterns.pattern: the rock cycle is a fixed one-way sequence (igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic, always in that order)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the cycle has many pathways and shortcuts — any type can become any other; it isn't a fixed conveyor. Trace several different routes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only in one fixed order — igneous first, then sedimentary, then metamorphic, never skipping.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: recites a single loop and can't describe shortcuts (e.g. metamorphic melting straight back to magma)

errorPatterns.pattern: metamorphic rock forms by melting (confused with igneous formation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Metamorphism changes rock by heat AND pressure WITHOUT fully melting (limestone→marble); melting then cooling makes IGNEOUS rock. Contrast the two directly.
errorPatterns.distractor: By melting the rock completely and letting it cool again.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says heat MELTS rock to make metamorphic rock, not distinguishing it from igneous

errorPatterns.pattern: geological processes are fast, on a human timescale ('it happens in a few years')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build deep-time intuition (mountains rise/erode over millions of years); that's why we see snapshots, not the process. Use timeline analogies.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects rock change to be observable quickly; no sense of millions of years

responseLevels.gap: Treats rocks as permanent; no notion of transformation or deep time; confuses metamorphism with melting.
responseLevels.full: Describes rock as continually recycled over geological time, traces specific routes between types (including shortcuts), distinguishes metamorphism from melting, and explains that the vast timescale is why we observe snapshots rather than the process.
responseLevels.partial: Names the three rock types and how each forms, but presents the cycle as a fixed one-way order or can't invoke geological time to explain why change is unseen — the parts without the dynamic, deep-time whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A student says 'rocks are permanent — a granite boulder is just always granite, it can't turn into any other kind of rock.' Is that true over a very long time? Then the important part: explain how a piece of one rock type could end up as a completely different type, and why we never see it happen.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who holds a dynamic, cyclic model over deep time from one who sees rocks as fixed and permanent (because change is never observed). Requiring a specific transformation route AND the timescale explanation is the discriminator — naming the three types isn't enough.
